CYBERBULLYING

By: Nicky Troll | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Bullying in the cyber world is a harsh reality for many South Africans – from children to celebrities and professionals, often with devastating consequences.

Summary:
It may have been designed with social connection in mind, but these days social media is less about friends, followers and sharing experiences. It has become a platform for cyberbullying, online harassment and trolling – and South Africa is one the main perpetrators.

We live in a digital world…. Gone are the days of things like going to the library, standing in line at the bank or writing an old friend a long letter with pen and paper… with technology at our finger tips – most things take place in a cyber world… even bullying.

The anonymity the internet offers, gives vindictive individuals the ability the verbally abuse and harass people without any real consequences or repercussions.

An underground world of trolls, flamers and cyberbullies are causing havoc on the internet that has devastating consequences in real life.

Carte Blanche looks at the dark side of social media.


Further information:
STATS
South Africa ranked number one in prevalence of cyberbullying among 28 countries pulled according to the latest Ipsos Global Advisor survey data. The other countries included Sweden, the US, Canada, Spain, Australia, the UK, Germany, Brazil, South Korea, Russia and Japan to name a few.

54% of South African parents know of a child in their community who has been the victim of cyber-bullying. 25% of SA parents said their own child had been bullied on digital platforms.

WHAT IS CYBERBULLYING
Bullying is no longer limited shove on the playground or random taunts in school corridors… it’s gone digital… text messages, social networking and instant messaging are the latest way to torment people.

The biggest frustration is that you can’t escape a cyberbully – it doesn’t end when you go home for the day... cyber bullies have access to you 24 hours a day through your phone, the internet... they don’t need to be physically in your face to harass you!

Cyber bullying can be anything from spreading rumors online or via text message to posting hurtful or threatening messages on social networking sites, web pages, via email and text message to Circulating sexually suggestive pictures or messages about a person.

While the initial abuse starts in a digital realm, the consequences of the abuse is real. Cyberbullies may not be in your face, but the torment still leaves a destructive trail . In some cases, the bullies have gone as far as encouraging people to commit suicide and tragically their victims have taken their own lives.

THE CULPRITS
People who have earned themselves these titles by launching tirades on the Internet, bad-mouthing anyone who comes in their way. But what are trolls, flamers, and cyber bullies?

Trolls are people who post non-relevant, often offensive content on message boards, forums, or social networking site—anywhere where they will get a reaction. Trolls often target particular websites or pages. Their victims are not usually known to them.
Cyberbullies use digital technology like the social networking, instant messaging or texting to intentionally hurt, humiliate, harass, intimidate or threaten another person. Cyber bullies target people they know in real life, in some cases not even bothering to use aliases.
Flamers use public forums as their stage to launch angry online fights – often at people unknown to them.
LEGALLY SPEAKING
The Protection from Harassment Act is often referred to as the cyberbullying law. If you are being threatened, harassed and / or stalked, in the real world or online, you can apply to get a protection order against that person.
In 2018, the National Assembly adopted the Cybercrimes and Cybersecurity Bill, which could see people face jail time for malicious online behaviour. This includes messages that incite or threaten violence and / or damage to property, and message containing intimate images that are sent without the person’s consent.
THERE’s EVEN SUCH A THING AS CYBER INSURANCE NOW
It’s gotten so bad, the extent of cyberbullying in South Africa has prompted women-centric insurer, 1st for Women, to launch the first cyberbullying insurance product in South Africa, which addresses the financial as well as legal burden of cyberbullying earlier this year.
A survey conducted by the insurer reinforces the magnitude of this growing problem, with 64% of the 4 000 participants believing that children were at risk.
“The costs of addressing cyberbullying can be astronomical, with lawyers charging around R3 000 an hour for consultations alone.
‘‘Also, in many instances, legal intervention is needed to put a stop to the bullying and bring the perpetrators to justice,” said Casey Rousseau from 1st for Women.
DEVASTING CONSEQUENCES
Rise in suicide cases in tandem with the rise of social media according to international statistics.

CASE STUDY 1
13-year old SUICIDE
This year, South Africa was rocked by the news that a 13 year old Pretoria school girl committed suicide after being bullied on whatsapp when a photo was sent around the school. It’s unclear what the image was of, but its alleged that learners had teased the girl about it. A grade 7 leaner had threatened to distribute a nude video of her online.

We speak to the young girl's mother - Liena Tubane.

CASE STUDY 2 – KARIMA BROWN - NOT DOING INTERVIEW _ BUT WE CAN REFER TO HER CASE...
Veteran journalist Karima Brown was the victim of attacks spurred on by the EFF’s Julius Malema in March this year.
Brown said she had been “threatened with rape, with sexual assault, with violence” after Malema shared her cellphone number in a tweet earlier this year.
“I was called a ‘whore’ and told people will deal with me. That I must leave the country and ‘f**k off back to India’,” she continued.
They included one saying she must “step aside or we will crush your prolapsed vagina,” one calling her “sfebe” [Zulu for bitch], one which appeared to be from an EFF supporter telling fellow EFF supporters to “go attack” her, one calling her a “coloured bitch” and a particularly long, gruesome message that included the author threatening to “peel that skin off ur pink bodies” [sic].
Brown said many of those who had threatened her were “clearly EFF members”, adding that she did, however, suspect some of the threats were sent by bots (fake accounts) or by those tweeting under a false identity or from multiple accounts (sometimes known as “sockpuppets”).
Karima won her case against the Economic Freedom Fighters and their leader Julius Malema after the high court ruled in her favour in June. The court found the EFF contravened the Electoral Code and must pay costs.
“It’s a scary time we live in when political parties can go unchecked, attacking female journalists for doing their jobs.”
CASE STUDY 3 – AMERICA GOPIE, THE BACHELOR CONTESTANT
I had been bullied for years over my teeth, so much so that I would refuse to leave the house. It was so damaging that three months before I was meant to join the reality TV show The Bachelor SA I had major reconstructive jaw surgery. It takes years to recover from this type of surgery, so when I entered the show, I was still a bit swollen and had to wear braces.
“Once the show aired, viewers started to tweet about my braces. Someone said, “America is so ugly, she need to go home, and don’t even get me started on her braces.” Antoher woman said, “She looks like she has bad breath.”

America says she cried for hours, after reading the negative comments on Twitter, Instagram and Youtube and refused to get out of bed the next day. “I felt hopeless but I just knew that I had to speak up, so I posted an article on Instagram addressing the bullying. After taking a stand against it, the support I received was overwhelming. I as inundated with love. While words have the power to destroy, we should remember they also have the power to heal.”

CYBER SECURITY EXPERT – CRAIG ROSEWARNE
Cyber bullies hide in a digital world. They are nameless and faceless – but their actions are real, devastating for the people on the receiving end.

Rosewarne speaks to the challenges in identifying cyber bullies and how to best safeguard yourself and your children against these cyber villans.


PSYCHOLOGIST EXPERT – HLENGIWE ZWANE
Dr Zwane specializes in treating adolescents – but also deals with adults. Cyber bullying is one of the areas she deals with extensively. She has a weekly slot on Kaya FM and speaks well.

LEGAL EXPERT
These cases are challenging to pursue legally because the legislation is new, the culprits are difficult to identify and sometime the evidence has been destroyed. A legal expert will give insights into these challenges.

Script:


STRUCTURE

VO: We live in a digital world of convenience – our lives are simpler and more efficient. But with the perks of connectivity, comes a dark side too - the cyber realm has given rise to a powerful breed of bully, far worse than the old school thug.

LINK: Bullying is no longer limited to a shove on the playground or random taunts in school corridors - it’s gone digital. Victims are tormented on social networking platforms – in the cyber world, everyone is a target.

VO: The Batchelor SA contestant, attorney America Gopie was at the receiving of end of cyberbullying when the show first aired in February this year.

AMERICA: I thought to myself, I still have braces on, here’s a platform for me to say to people, regardless of what you look like , you can still put yourself out there, it doesn’t preclude you from finding love.

VO: But viewers were not supportive or complementary – they took too social media to criticise and insult America’s physical appearance.

AMERICA: It got really nasty – in episode 4 I was just trending for being ugly. America’s teeth are so terrible, people are let not even get started on the braces.

VO: America wore braces during the show following an 8-hour reconstructive jaw operation that corrected a severe overbite that made her the target of real life bullies as a child.

AMERICA: And then in episode 5 I kissed Lee on our one on one date – oh my gosh that kiss looked so painful – America look like she has such bad breath, how did Lee do that.

VO: While the abuse is mentally taxing on the victims it doesn’t appear to deter the culprits explains Psychologist Ilze Alberts.

ILZE: The digital world has made it far to easy to hide behind a screen and to intentionally damage and hurt another person.

AMERICA: I really thought that my bullying stopped in school and here I was facing the whole things over again.

LINK: The torment is relentless - you don’t know when it’s going strike and very often the culprits are faceless – difficult to catch and hold accountable - for the victim it means there is no escape.

VO: Technology attorney Russell Luck explains that cyberbullying is constant – it’s 24/7. It ranges from pictures and videos to memes and derogatory language – sometimes it doesn’t even have to be real – malicious content can be fabricated.

RUSSELL: Cyberbullying is not just one type of behaviour – it refers to a spectrum of acts, if in terms of your cyberbullying or in the online domain you are engaging in words or conducts that would constitute harassment, hate speech or crimen injuria – yes it’s a crime //

VO: The targets of cyberbullying experience a genuine sense of torment.

ILZE: There is a form of depression that comes in, and that feeling of helplessness, hopelessness, and a deep feeling of loneliness, the world is against me.

VO: For America, the unrelenting comments brought back memories of past trauma.

AMERICA:….. I didn’t even want to go to work….

VO: When it comes to bullying, the cyber world is much scarier than the real world according to Cyber Security Expert Craig Rosewarne.

CRAIG: In cyber space you can be anyone, you can spoof a telephone number, you can spoof an sms, an email, you can change your voice // cyber space and the dark web creates a beautiful hiding place for these bullies to actually operate from.
DEVI: Which makes it easier for the bully
CRAIG: It gives people this voice to reach millions of people out there and say what they want to say –people always they and be controversial and people are mean at the end of day.

VO: This, is the coward’s way of bullying - vengeful from a distance.

ILZE: knowing I don’t have to face this person is giving a huge sense of power and a huge sense of control – so that is that grandiose feeling I have this impact on another human being.

LINK: With anonymity, cyber attacks often gain momentum quickly - this breed of bully believes think they are untouchable. Because they are disconnected from the impact of their actions in the digitial world.

VO: Fearlessly outspoken political analyst and journalist Karima Brown was subjected to a viral digital attack of abuse which included graphic rape and death threats after EFF party leader, Julius Malema, blasted her personal contact number on Twitter, alleging that Brown was attempting to spy on the EFF.

Many cyber bulies mistakingly think they are above the law explains Luck.

RUSSELL: People must remember that what you do in the digital world is not different from the physical world and you will be held accountable.

VO: In Brown’s case, there was a clear instigator. She took the EFF to court, because the attacks started, when Malema seemingly invited his Twitter followers to harass her.

The courted ruled in her favour – The judge found that the EFF had violated the electoral code by failing to “instruct and take reasonable steps to ensure that their supporters do not harass, intimidate, threaten or abuse journalists and especially women”.

ILZE: She did not allow them to bully her, she is a role model for many people

VO: While this was a relatively clear cut case – bringing the culprits to book can be challenging more often than not according to Luck.

RUSSELL: It’s not so much about having inadequate laws, it’s about having inadequate enforcement because somewhere between the law and the machinery that follows those laws and implement them things get lost in the ether.

VO: But this shouldn’t deter victims from reporting these cases and taking investigations further – there are means and ways advises Rosewarne.

DEVI:
CRAIG: if we get the IP address then it is gotcha…

VO: But even with human rights, legislation and cyber tools this type of abuse often causes a devastating trail of destruction – especially where the targets are young.

Linah Tubane’s 13 year old daughter Angel was the focus of a combined cyber and real life bullying attack at her school.

LINAH: She started to behave strangely – she will shout at her little sister // she would come in and go to her bedroom and close her door - not like angel was

VO: Angel failed the previous year and would have to repeat the grade. She sent her mom a voice note about a girl a school that was teasing her.

UPSOUND VOICE NOTE
And this situation is making me emotional, because she is busy saying she is going to embarrass me.

VO: Apparently there was also a video circulating amongst some learners at the school of Angel doing a popular dance called twerking.

UPSOUND VOICE NOTE
And now she is busy telling people that I am a whore and I’m doing lots of things

VO: She didn’t tell her mom about the video, but reported the bullying to a teacher - no action was taken and the bullying continued.

The new Cybercrimes and Cybersecurity Bill aims to deliver more serious consequences for transgressions in the digital realm – but is yet to be enacted.

RUSSELL: The law can never regulate in accordance with the speed of which technology evolves, // by the time the cyber crime bill is actually enacted as legislation new instances of bullying and online wrongfulness will occur

VO: But for children legislation has very little impact on the daily trauma they experience at the hands of bullies.

It got so bad for Linah’s daughter Angel – that she refused to go to school. Linah went to see the principal who insisted that she should bring her daughter in.

But Angel refused point blank.

LINAH: I tried to speak to her and I was calm – she was so angry – I never seen her so angry //she went outside, came back into her bedroom – and went outside and that’s when she went outside for the last time – that is when she killed her self. 09.26

VO: It was all too much for Angel – she took her own life at the age of 13.

Physiologically teenagers are not equipped to deal with these types of challenges, as the prefrontal cortex of their brains, dealing with rational thought processing, has not fully developed explains Alberts.

ILZE: // it takes time for the brain to fully develop that logical thinking // so I will go and hang myself but I am not going to die. // that is the magical thinking of teenagers, that they are invincible and that what is happening to other human beings as a consequence is not going to happen to themselves.

VO: But the consequences of Angel’s death are very real for her mother.

LINAH: I think I am a bad parent – why didn’t I see this think coming – I blamed my self – I asked myself a lot of questions // It has changed my life – because I have lost angel –








PROMOS

PROMO 1
VO: In the playground of the cyberbully, there are no merry-go-rounds – there are no swings and no slides, but there’s an endless possibility to do harm in the digital realm.

PROMO 2
VO: A video of a 13-year old girl dancing goes viral. She becomes the target of cyberbullies – tormented and embarrassed by her attackers - the consequences were devastating.

PROMO 3
VO: Bullying has gone digital. Taunts and insults wielded from behind a screen makes everyone is a potential target– but how do you fight an invisible tormentor in the cyber realm?

Carte Blanche HD nombuso@carteblanche.co.za 12 August 2019 Script: STRUCTURE VO: We live in a digital world of convenience – our lives are simpler and more efficient. But with the perks of connectivity, comes a dark side too - the cyber realm has given rise to a powerful breed of bully, far worse than the old school thug. LINK: Bullying is no longer limited to a shove on the playground or random taunts in school corridors - it’s gone digital. Victims are tormented on social networking platforms – in the cyber world, everyone is a target. VO: The Batchelor SA contestant, attorney America Gopie was at the receiving of end of cyberbullying when the show first aired in February this year. AMERICA: I thought to myself, I still have braces on, here’s a platform for me to say to people, regardless of what you look like , you can still put yourself out there, it doesn’t preclude you from finding love. VO: But viewers were not supportive or complementary – they took too social media to criticise and insult America’s physical appearance. AMERICA: It got really nasty – in episode 4 I was just trending for being ugly. America’s teeth are so terrible, people are let not even get started on the braces. VO: America wore braces during the show following an 8-hour reconstructive jaw operation that corrected a severe overbite that made her the target of real life bullies as a child. AMERICA: And then in episode 5 I kissed Lee on our one on one date – oh my gosh that kiss looked so painful – America look like she has such bad breath, how did Lee do that. VO: While the abuse is mentally taxing on the victims it doesn’t appear to deter the culprits explains Psychologist Ilze Alberts. ILZE: The digital world has made it far to easy to hide behind a screen and to intentionally damage and hurt another person. AMERICA: I really thought that my bullying stopped in school and here I was facing the whole things over again. LINK: The torment is relentless - you don’t know when it’s going strike and very often the culprits are faceless – difficult to catch and hold accountable - for the victim it means there is no escape. VO: Technology attorney Russell Luck explains that cyberbullying is constant – it’s 24/7. It ranges from pictures and videos to memes and derogatory language – sometimes it doesn’t even have to be real – malicious content can be fabricated. RUSSELL: Cyberbullying is not just one type of behaviour – it refers to a spectrum of acts, if in terms of your cyberbullying or in the online domain you are engaging in words or conducts that would constitute harassment, hate speech or crimen injuria – yes it’s a crime // VO: The targets of cyberbullying experience a genuine sense of torment. ILZE: There is a form of depression that comes in, and that feeling of helplessness, hopelessness, and a deep feeling of loneliness, the world is against me. VO: For America, the unrelenting comments brought back memories of past trauma. AMERICA:….. I didn’t even want to go to work…. VO: When it comes to bullying, the cyber world is much scarier than the real world according to Cyber Security Expert Craig Rosewarne. CRAIG: In cyber space you can be anyone, you can spoof a telephone number, you can spoof an sms, an email, you can change your voice // cyber space and the dark web creates a beautiful hiding place for these bullies to actually operate from. DEVI: Which makes it easier for the bully CRAIG: It gives people this voice to reach millions of people out there and say what they want to say –people always they and be controversial and people are mean at the end of day. VO: This, is the coward’s way of bullying - vengeful from a distance. ILZE: knowing I don’t have to face this person is giving a huge sense of power and a huge sense of control – so that is that grandiose feeling I have this impact on another human being. LINK: With anonymity, cyber attacks often gain momentum quickly - this breed of bully believes think they are untouchable. Because they are disconnected from the impact of their actions in the digitial world. VO: Fearlessly outspoken political analyst and journalist Karima Brown was subjected to a viral digital attack of abuse which included graphic rape and death threats after EFF party leader, Julius Malema, blasted her personal contact number on Twitter, alleging that Brown was attempting to spy on the EFF. Many cyber bulies mistakingly think they are above the law explains Luck. RUSSELL: People must remember that what you do in the digital world is not different from the physical world and you will be held accountable. VO: In Brown’s case, there was a clear instigator. She took the EFF to court, because the attacks started, when Malema seemingly invited his Twitter followers to harass her. The courted ruled in her favour – The judge found that the EFF had violated the electoral code by failing to “instruct and take reasonable steps to ensure that their supporters do not harass, intimidate, threaten or abuse journalists and especially women”. ILZE: She did not allow them to bully her, she is a role model for many people VO: While this was a relatively clear cut case – bringing the culprits to book can be challenging more often than not according to Luck. RUSSELL: It’s not so much about having inadequate laws, it’s about having inadequate enforcement because somewhere between the law and the machinery that follows those laws and implement them things get lost in the ether. VO: But this shouldn’t deter victims from reporting these cases and taking investigations further – there are means and ways advises Rosewarne. DEVI: CRAIG: if we get the IP address then it is gotcha… VO: But even with human rights, legislation and cyber tools this type of abuse often causes a devastating trail of destruction – especially where the targets are young. Linah Tubane’s 13 year old daughter Angel was the focus of a combined cyber and real life bullying attack at her school. LINAH: She started to behave strangely – she will shout at her little sister // she would come in and go to her bedroom and close her door - not like angel was VO: Angel failed the previous year and would have to repeat the grade. She sent her mom a voice note about a girl a school that was teasing her. UPSOUND VOICE NOTE And this situation is making me emotional, because she is busy saying she is going to embarrass me. VO: Apparently there was also a video circulating amongst some learners at the school of Angel doing a popular dance called twerking. UPSOUND VOICE NOTE And now she is busy telling people that I am a whore and I’m doing lots of things VO: She didn’t tell her mom about the video, but reported the bullying to a teacher - no action was taken and the bullying continued. The new Cybercrimes and Cybersecurity Bill aims to deliver more serious consequences for transgressions in the digital realm – but is yet to be enacted. RUSSELL: The law can never regulate in accordance with the speed of which technology evolves, // by the time the cyber crime bill is actually enacted as legislation new instances of bullying and online wrongfulness will occur VO: But for children legislation has very little impact on the daily trauma they experience at the hands of bullies. It got so bad for Linah’s daughter Angel – that she refused to go to school. Linah went to see the principal who insisted that she should bring her daughter in. But Angel refused point blank. LINAH: I tried to speak to her and I was calm – she was so angry – I never seen her so angry //she went outside, came back into her bedroom – and went outside and that’s when she went outside for the last time – that is when she killed her self. 09.26 VO: It was all too much for Angel – she took her own life at the age of 13. Physiologically teenagers are not equipped to deal with these types of challenges, as the prefrontal cortex of their brains, dealing with rational thought processing, has not fully developed explains Alberts. ILZE: // it takes time for the brain to fully develop that logical thinking // so I will go and hang myself but I am not going to die. // that is the magical thinking of teenagers, that they are invincible and that what is happening to other human beings as a consequence is not going to happen to themselves. VO: But the consequences of Angel’s death are very real for her mother. LINAH: I think I am a bad parent – why didn’t I see this think coming – I blamed my self – I asked myself a lot of questions // It has changed my life – because I have lost angel – PROMOS PROMO 1 VO: In the playground of the cyberbully, there are no merry-go-rounds – there are no swings and no slides, but there’s an endless possibility to do harm in the digital realm. PROMO 2 VO: A video of a 13-year old girl dancing goes viral. She becomes the target of cyberbullies – tormented and embarrassed by her attackers - the consequences were devastating. PROMO 3 VO: Bullying has gone digital. Taunts and insults wielded from behind a screen makes everyone is a potential target– but how do you fight an invisible tormentor in the cyber realm?

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Bullying in the cyber world is a harsh reality for many South Africans – from children to celebrities and professionals, often with devastating consequences.
metadata.Summary: It may have been designed with social connection in mind, but these days social media is less about friends, followers and sharing experiences. It has become a platform for cyberbullying, online harassment and trolling – and South Africa is one the main perpetrators. We live in a digital world…. Gone are the days of things like going to the library, standing in line at the bank or writing an old friend a long letter with pen and paper… with technology at our finger tips – most things take place in a cyber world… even bullying. The anonymity the internet offers, gives vindictive individuals the ability the verbally abuse and harass people without any real consequences or repercussions. An underground world of trolls, flamers and cyberbullies are causing havoc on the internet that has devastating consequences in real life. Carte Blanche looks at the dark side of social media.
metadata.Further information: STATS South Africa ranked number one in prevalence of cyberbullying among 28 countries pulled according to the latest Ipsos Global Advisor survey data. The other countries included Sweden, the US, Canada, Spain, Australia, the UK, Germany, Brazil, South Korea, Russia and Japan to name a few. 54% of South African parents know of a child in their community who has been the victim of cyber-bullying. 25% of SA parents said their own child had been bullied on digital platforms. WHAT IS CYBERBULLYING Bullying is no longer limited shove on the playground or random taunts in school corridors… it’s gone digital… text messages, social networking and instant messaging are the latest way to torment people. The biggest frustration is that you can’t escape a cyberbully – it doesn’t end when you go home for the day... cyber bullies have access to you 24 hours a day through your phone, the internet... they don’t need to be physically in your face to harass you! Cyber bullying can be anything from spreading rumors online or via text message to posting hurtful or threatening messages on social networking sites, web pages, via email and text message to Circulating sexually suggestive pictures or messages about a person. While the initial abuse starts in a digital realm, the consequences of the abuse is real. Cyberbullies may not be in your face, but the torment still leaves a destructive trail . In some cases, the bullies have gone as far as encouraging people to commit suicide and tragically their victims have taken their own lives. THE CULPRITS People who have earned themselves these titles by launching tirades on the Internet, bad-mouthing anyone who comes in their way. But what are trolls, flamers, and cyber bullies? Trolls are people who post non-relevant, often offensive content on message boards, forums, or social networking site—anywhere where they will get a reaction. Trolls often target particular websites or pages. Their victims are not usually known to them. Cyberbullies use digital technology like the social networking, instant messaging or texting to intentionally hurt, humiliate, harass, intimidate or threaten another person. Cyber bullies target people they know in real life, in some cases not even bothering to use aliases. Flamers use public forums as their stage to launch angry online fights – often at people unknown to them. LEGALLY SPEAKING The Protection from Harassment Act is often referred to as the cyberbullying law. If you are being threatened, harassed and / or stalked, in the real world or online, you can apply to get a protection order against that person. In 2018, the National Assembly adopted the Cybercrimes and Cybersecurity Bill, which could see people face jail time for malicious online behaviour. This includes messages that incite or threaten violence and / or damage to property, and message containing intimate images that are sent without the person’s consent. THERE’s EVEN SUCH A THING AS CYBER INSURANCE NOW It’s gotten so bad, the extent of cyberbullying in South Africa has prompted women-centric insurer, 1st for Women, to launch the first cyberbullying insurance product in South Africa, which addresses the financial as well as legal burden of cyberbullying earlier this year. A survey conducted by the insurer reinforces the magnitude of this growing problem, with 64% of the 4 000 participants believing that children were at risk. “The costs of addressing cyberbullying can be astronomical, with lawyers charging around R3 000 an hour for consultations alone. ‘‘Also, in many instances, legal intervention is needed to put a stop to the bullying and bring the perpetrators to justice,” said Casey Rousseau from 1st for Women. DEVASTING CONSEQUENCES Rise in suicide cases in tandem with the rise of social media according to international statistics. CASE STUDY 1 13-year old SUICIDE This year, South Africa was rocked by the news that a 13 year old Pretoria school girl committed suicide after being bullied on whatsapp when a photo was sent around the school. It’s unclear what the image was of, but its alleged that learners had teased the girl about it. A grade 7 leaner had threatened to distribute a nude video of her online. We speak to the young girl's mother - Liena Tubane. CASE STUDY 2 – KARIMA BROWN - NOT DOING INTERVIEW _ BUT WE CAN REFER TO HER CASE... Veteran journalist Karima Brown was the victim of attacks spurred on by the EFF’s Julius Malema in March this year. Brown said she had been “threatened with rape, with sexual assault, with violence” after Malema shared her cellphone number in a tweet earlier this year. “I was called a ‘whore’ and told people will deal with me. That I must leave the country and ‘f**k off back to India’,” she continued. They included one saying she must “step aside or we will crush your prolapsed vagina,” one calling her “sfebe” [Zulu for bitch], one which appeared to be from an EFF supporter telling fellow EFF supporters to “go attack” her, one calling her a “coloured bitch” and a particularly long, gruesome message that included the author threatening to “peel that skin off ur pink bodies” [sic]. Brown said many of those who had threatened her were “clearly EFF members”, adding that she did, however, suspect some of the threats were sent by bots (fake accounts) or by those tweeting under a false identity or from multiple accounts (sometimes known as “sockpuppets”). Karima won her case against the Economic Freedom Fighters and their leader Julius Malema after the high court ruled in her favour in June. The court found the EFF contravened the Electoral Code and must pay costs. “It’s a scary time we live in when political parties can go unchecked, attacking female journalists for doing their jobs.” CASE STUDY 3 – AMERICA GOPIE, THE BACHELOR CONTESTANT I had been bullied for years over my teeth, so much so that I would refuse to leave the house. It was so damaging that three months before I was meant to join the reality TV show The Bachelor SA I had major reconstructive jaw surgery. It takes years to recover from this type of surgery, so when I entered the show, I was still a bit swollen and had to wear braces. “Once the show aired, viewers started to tweet about my braces. Someone said, “America is so ugly, she need to go home, and don’t even get me started on her braces.” Antoher woman said, “She looks like she has bad breath.” America says she cried for hours, after reading the negative comments on Twitter, Instagram and Youtube and refused to get out of bed the next day. “I felt hopeless but I just knew that I had to speak up, so I posted an article on Instagram addressing the bullying. After taking a stand against it, the support I received was overwhelming. I as inundated with love. While words have the power to destroy, we should remember they also have the power to heal.” CYBER SECURITY EXPERT – CRAIG ROSEWARNE Cyber bullies hide in a digital world. They are nameless and faceless – but their actions are real, devastating for the people on the receiving end. Rosewarne speaks to the challenges in identifying cyber bullies and how to best safeguard yourself and your children against these cyber villans. PSYCHOLOGIST EXPERT – HLENGIWE ZWANE Dr Zwane specializes in treating adolescents – but also deals with adults. Cyber bullying is one of the areas she deals with extensively. She has a weekly slot on Kaya FM and speaks well. LEGAL EXPERT These cases are challenging to pursue legally because the legislation is new, the culprits are difficult to identify and sometime the evidence has been destroyed. A legal expert will give insights into these challenges.
